findings.claim: Retailers use mark-up to ensure they cover costs and generate a profit on every item sold.
findings.truth: A mark-up above cost price creates gross profit on an item, but it cannot ensure that all overheads are covered or that the business makes net profit.
findings.evidence: Fetched Wikipedia Gross income page: gross profit is before overheads, payroll, tax and interest. The lesson's £5-to-£8 example leaves £3 before other costs.

findings.claim: This means Store A converts its footfall into sales much more effectively.
findings.truth: With identical footfall, the figures show that Store A earns more revenue per visitor. They do not establish conversion rate, which needs purchaser or transaction data.
findings.evidence: Recomputation: £22,400 ÷ 5,600 = £4.00 per visitor; £14,000 ÷ 5,600 = £2.50. Fetched Wikipedia Conversion marketing page defines conversion rate as goal achievements divided by visitors.

findings.claim: relying solely on online growth risks sacrificing the higher-margin in-store sales
findings.truth: The data show a higher average in-store transaction value (£62 versus £38), not a higher profit margin. No cost or profit data are supplied.
findings.evidence: The practice-question data state average transaction values only; profit margin requires profit and revenue figures.

summary: Three verified, surgical corrections address one accounting overclaim and two unsupported model-answer inferences.
